stories.headline: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification: with about 90% of its code written by Claude, the checks are now the job
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it, it is climbing Hacker News, and it is the clearest playbook yet for running many agents in parallel without reviewing every diff yourself.
body: The Claude Code team says roughly 90% of its code is now written and reviewed by Claude, so the real engineering problem has become giving agents ways to prove their work with evidence. Their argument: without verification loops you can only babysit one or two agents at a time; with them you can run dozens or hundreds. In internal tests on structured file generation, a separate grader checking Claude's output against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points, with the biggest gains on the hardest problems. Tests, benchmarks and specs that used to be expensive to write are now cheap to ask an agent for, and once written they run as ordinary software.

The post names three kinds of tests worth investing in, starting with end-to-end tests of real user flows, and then property and differential tests. It also warns about failure modes that train agents badly: flaky tests teach an agent to rerun instead of fix, and slow tests mean fewer checks per batch. The same idea showed up at Vercel Ship SF, where Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke told Guillermo Rauch that "we are now all verification engineers", building harnesses, acceptance tests and "verifiables".

stories.headline: Cybercab is coming to Giga Berlin: Tesla commits about €3 billion to a new factory hall, with production expected to start in 2029
stories.why_read: It is the first Cybercab production commitment outside Texas, straight from the Giga Berlin plant manager, and it says Tesla is planning for robotaxi volume, not a pilot.
body: André Thierig, who runs Tesla's Giga Berlin plant, announced a first investment of around €3 billion in a new manufacturing building at the site in Grünheide for Cybercab production, with start of production anticipated in 2029. He said it will have the most advanced technology of any Tesla factory and that the plant is hiring. The announcement answers a long-running question about what Tesla would do with the large unused land around the factory.

X News coverage of the announcement reports a target of up to one million Cybercabs a year by 2029 and a building roughly twice the size of the current main hall, alongside existing Model Y output. Those capacity figures come from summaries of the coverage rather than Tesla's own post, so treat them as reported, not confirmed.

stories.headline: SemiAnalysis slashes its AI accelerator spending forecast by up to 41%, and Nvidia falls more than 5% before the open
stories.why_read: If you track inference economics, this is the most important forecast revision of the year: a $608 billion cut to 2030 alone, with Nvidia taking most of the hit.
body: Semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis lowered its global AI accelerator capex forecasts sharply: 2027 from $770 billion to $627 billion, 2028 from $1.054 trillion to $758 billion, 2029 from $1.352 trillion to $796 billion and 2030 from $1.531 trillion to $923 billion. It also cut its cumulative 2026-2030 accelerator silicon shipment forecast by 17%, with Nvidia accounting for 66% of that reduction, trimmed 2028 HBM shipments from 9.0 to 6.4 exabytes and cut projected 2030 AI accelerator power demand from 122.8 GW to 80.7 GW. The firm pointed to slowing revenue growth at frontier labs, tighter capital markets and lower chip and memory pricing.

The Kobeissi Letter reported that Nvidia fell more than 5% in Monday premarket trading, pulling Nasdaq 100 futures down 1.7%, and that it has erased nearly $2 trillion in market cap since its October 6 peak. Even after the cuts, SemiAnalysis still expects annual accelerator spending to more than double by 2030, so this is a slower curve, not a reversal.

stories.headline: Windows 11 quietly tracks which coding agents you run, from claude.exe and codex.exe to cursor.exe, and reports it to Microsoft by default
stories.why_read: If you run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor on Windows, this is a concrete look at what your OS reports about your toolchain, found by an AI-assisted reverse-engineering pass.
body: Xusheng Li asked an AI agent to comb the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and it surfaced MissionControlAggregator.dll, which holds explicit executable names for coding agents. There are four CLI-agent slots checking copilot.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe and agy.exe, with WSL equivalents, and five desktop-agent slots for github.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, cursor.exe and antigravity.exe, behind a feature flag literally named CLICodingAgentUsage. The component records which agents were used, saves that locally and reports it to Windows Diagnostics.

The list goes well beyond AI: node, python, dotnet, gcc, clang, gdb, javac, Visual Studio and VS Code are all checked, some with publisher verification. Unless you have opted out of optional diagnostic data, which is on by default, the data is uploaded to Microsoft. The Hacker News thread passed 600 points and nearly 500 comments overnight.

stories.headline: Optimizely's CDN served malware to visitors of 178 organisations, including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab and HSBC
stories.why_read: A textbook third-party JavaScript supply-chain attack: none of the victims' own servers were breached, and the payload stole crypto, cards and cookies.
body: On November 16, attackers wrote their own code into the Project JavaScript field of Optimizely Web customer projects, so the malicious loader was served from cdn.optimizely.com with Optimizely's certificate, from a host every affected site already trusted. Report URI says 178 organisations were hit, among them Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock. The kit swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits. Crypto has already been stolen.

Report URI saw three variants of the injected loader, including one hidden in base64, and Smartsheet's snippet was cleaned and then re-infected. By 21:52 UTC the code remained in only 1 of 188 infected snippets, down from 169 an hour earlier. The lesson is the uncomfortable one for architects: trusted JavaScript does not stay trusted, and only a strict CSP or script-change monitoring would have caught it.

stories.headline: SpaceX posts the view from Mechazilla of the first ever Starship catch, and fans can see the chopsticks scrape the ablative
stories.why_read: You retweeted the close-up overnight; the tower-cam footage is the best look yet at what a ship catch actually does to the vehicle.
body: SpaceX released two clips shot from Mechazilla itself during the first ever Starship catch, and the post passed 31,000 likes. Robin (@xdNiBoR), in a post you retweeted, pointed out that you can see the ablative coating being scraped off where the chopsticks grab the ship.

The other detail people keep coming back to is the heat shield. Everyday Astronaut noted that Starship carries about 18,000 tiles and only one fell off on this flight, roughly a 99.995% hold rate, and expects SpaceX to keep chasing more nines until a missing tile is rare.

stories.headline: Anthropic has reportedly passed the US government as SpaceX's top customer
stories.why_read: It is a one-line report with big implications: compute and connectivity for an AI lab now outweigh the Pentagon and NASA on SpaceX's books.
body: Unusual Whales, citing Yahoo Finance, reported Monday that Anthropic has overtaken the US government as SpaceX's largest customer. The post drew more than 6,000 likes and you bookmarked it.

The report did not break out what Anthropic is buying or how much, so the details are still thin. But the direction fits the past few weeks of SpaceX news, where AI customers and AI-linked investors keep showing up next to launch and Starlink in the story of what the company is becoming.

stories.headline: Databricks AI Index: open-weight models jumped from 7.3% to 30.9% of enterprise token traffic in about three and a half months
stories.why_read: Real gateway traffic from more than 10,000 companies, not a survey, and it says open-weight models and multi-model routing are now mainstream in the enterprise.
body: Databricks co-founder Patrick Wendell published the first Databricks AI Index, built from enterprises that manage AI through its Unity Gateway, covering more than 10,000 companies across digital natives, the Fortune 500 and the Global 2000. X News coverage of the release reports that open-weight models went from 7.3% to 30.9% of token traffic in roughly 3.5 months.

The same coverage says 75% of firms now use two or more model providers and half use three or more, with DeepSeek and Zhipu models popular for coding and batch work, and task routing such as one model for planning and another for editing becoming standard. For anyone architecting an internal AI gateway, that is a strong signal to design for many models from day one.

stories.headline: JPMorgan says robotaxi could be 40% of Tesla's long-term value, citing a Texas fleet that has nearly caught Waymo
stories.why_read: A neutral-rated bank putting a big number on Robotaxi is a useful outside check on the Austin progress you follow so closely.
body: According to X News coverage, JPMorgan kept a neutral rating on Tesla with a $430 price target while crediting Robotaxi for about 40% of the company's 2035 valuation. The note highlights Tesla's Texas fleet, reported at 1,306 vehicles, roughly matching Waymo's, and about 50% of Austin's autonomous miles despite a later start, with unsupervised miles reported at 5.3 million.

The bank expects national parity with Waymo by late 2027 and meaningful revenue from 2028. Separately, Elon Musk replied "Of course" to an investor arguing that moderate Cybercab success is already priced into Tesla's roughly $1.5 trillion valuation. All figures here are as reported in coverage of the note, not from the note itself.

stories.headline: "Strictly better than Waymo": a first Cybercab ride in Austin, and a case that robotaxis will eat short-haul flights
stories.why_read: You retweeted both: one rider's first impression from your own city, and a back-of-the-envelope argument for why door-to-door autonomy beats a regional flight.
body: Steve Hou rode Tesla's Robotaxi in Austin for the first time and called Cybercab strictly better than Waymo: a smoother ride, a better-smelling cabin and "not particularly close", comparing the two to Mac and PC.

Chris First took the idea further. Flying to Boston, he estimates, is 5 to 5.5 hours door to door once you add the drive to the airport, TSA, bags and the ride into town, while a robotaxi from his door would take about 4 hours and let him work or sleep the whole way. Cross-country will still mean flying, he says, but flights to nearby states are "toast".

stories.headline: A first pass at the new NHTSA data: in Texas driverless incidents, Tesla and Waymo look statistically the same relative to fleet size
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it; it is an honest amateur analysis that says what the data can and cannot show.
body: James Cat (@TSLAFanMtl) filtered the newest NHTSA crash report to Texas and to incidents with no driver in the vehicle, then lined Tesla and Waymo incidents up against each company's fleet growth over time. His conclusion: no statistical difference between the two in incidents relative to fleet size.

He is upfront about the limitation. NHTSA does not report miles driven or utilization for each service, so incidents per mile, the measure that really matters, cannot be computed from this release. Read it as a sanity check, not a verdict.

stories.headline: Grok Bot 1.0 arrives with bots that join your meetings and take initiative, and SpaceX lights up the Las Vegas Sphere to sell it
stories.why_read: This is the product you live in every day; Matt Palmer's walkthrough covers what changed, and the Sphere ad shows how hard SpaceX is pushing it.
body: Matt Palmer posted a tour of what is new in Grok Bot 1.0: team bot improvements, bots that join your meetings, bots that take initiative, bots that learn and improve, and bots that are smarter and faster. X News coverage describes shared team bots that work across Slack, Microsoft Teams, Zoom and Google Meet, and points to a November 11 changelog covering meeting integrations and approval flows. Parker Smith at SpaceXAI is now asking heavy users who automate most of their work with Bot to share how they use it, in exchange for credits.

On the marketing side, the official @bot account posted "Every driver needs their crew" with footage of Grok Bot faces on the exterior of the Las Vegas Sphere, timed to the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend. Han Wang summed up the mood in a post you retweeted: Grok Bot is doing to everyone else what Claude Code did to coding agents.

stories.headline: Grok Bot sat through a 90-minute AT&T support call, and the agent who called back was stunned she had been talking to a bot
stories.why_read: Two field reports from heavy users, one on the phone and one on a 500-mile FSD drive, that show what agents feel like when they work.
body: DJ (@congressdj) says Grok Bot handled a complex 90-minute phone call with AT&T for him, which is the current time limit for Grok Bot calls. When AT&T called back, the agent was stunned to learn she had been speaking with a bot the whole time, said other bots had called before but "nothing like this", and downloaded Grok Bot while still on the line.

In a post you retweeted, Mike P describes a 500-mile drive from Philadelphia to the South Carolina border on FSD: taking a meeting at a Supercharger stop, having Grok Bot summarize it into markdown and send it to colleagues, and using "Hey Grok" in the car to put follow-up meetings on his calendar. FSD removes the driving stress, he writes, and Grok Bot lets him keep up with his day from the driver's seat.

stories.headline: OpenRouter's weekly token volume went from about 7 trillion to about 210 trillion in a year, roughly 30x
stories.why_read: You retweeted it, and it lines up with the Monday leaderboard you track: one chart that captures how fast inference demand is compounding.
body: Trade Whisperer charted OpenRouter's weekly token usage over the past year: about 7 trillion tokens a week in November 2025 and about 210 trillion a week in November 2026, roughly a 30x increase. "This is year one," the post says.

Read it next to today's SemiAnalysis forecast cut. Demand for tokens keeps exploding even as analysts trim how much money will go into accelerators, which mostly says the cost per token is falling fast.

stories.headline: Cursor's David Gomes: Projects are "insane" but only about 40% of where they should be, and you made the case for making them the only entity
stories.why_read: Your own reply is in this one: you argued Cursor should drop the split between local folders and cloud Projects.
body: David Gomes of Cursor says Cursor Projects are a big improvement over Agents and Chats and worth adopting now, but still only about 40% of where he thinks they will end up, so the team needs time to iron out the edges. Eric Zakariasson also shipped a small quality-of-life change: voice prompts can now go straight to the agent without a second click to send.

You replied to David that Projects should be the only domain object Cursor offers, arguing that the current split, with "Open Folder or Workspace" for local work and Projects for cloud or remote work, is a seam that should go away.

stories.headline: Theo: Fable 5.2 is the first model that consistently ignores unimportant feedback, plus Claude Code can now fold an iPhone Duo in the simulator
stories.why_read: Two quick model and tool notes you retweeted last night, both about agents getting better judgment and better test surfaces.
body: Theo says Fable 5.2 is the first model that reliably ignores feedback that does not matter. He had at least a dozen threads where Opus started running in circles, and switching to Fable produced the equivalent of "this is fine, just ship it".

Separately, ClaudeDevs announced that Claude Code on desktop now supports the iPhone Duo in the iOS simulator in public beta. You can run your app on a Duo next to the conversation, and Claude can fold and unfold the device to test each layout, which is exactly the kind of cheap verification loop the Claude Code team writes about today.

stories.headline: OpenCode Browse lets coding agents drive your real browser, with your tabs, logins and extensions, and hand the tab back for 2FA
stories.why_read: It is a clean design for the hardest part of browser agents, logins and payments, and it works with Claude Code, Cursor and Codex as well as OpenCode.
body: OpenCode Browse is an MCP server plus a Chromium extension. Agents open tabs in the background in collapsed groups, then read pages, click, type, take screenshots and record tabs and network traffic. When a login, 2FA prompt or payment comes up, they hand the tab back to you and continue when you click Continue. You can also lend an agent a tab you already have open, and restrict an agent to sites you name.

It supports Chrome, Edge, Brave, Arc, Helium, Vivaldi, Opera and Chromium, and any MCP client, including OpenCode, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and Zed. The trade-off is the obvious one: agents inherit every site you are signed into, so the allowed-sites setting matters.

stories.headline: Harmonic's Aristotle can now formally prove Rust code has no undefined behavior, even inside unsafe blocks
stories.why_read: Same theme as today's lead, taken to the extreme: if AI writes the code, prove it correct instead of only testing it.
body: Harmonic extended Aristotle, which already covers C and Verilog, to Rust. It can prove that code has no undefined behavior and does exactly what its spec says, including inside unsafe blocks, and when you rewrite C in Rust it can prove the new code behaves the same as the original. CEO Tudor Achim framed it bluntly: Rust is where much of the world's critical new code is being written, and increasingly AI is writing it.

Harmonic is partnering with the Solana Foundation. On the open-source Manifest order book, Aristotle proved 28 results and found a rounding bug that has since been fixed. A companion Hacker News favorite, "Formal Verification Is Not Verifiable", is a good counterweight on what a proof does and does not guarantee.

stories.headline: Mitchell Hashimoto unveils Rex, his long-promised answer to "Vagrant for remote environments"
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it: the creator of Vagrant and Terraform says he finally got remote development right after years of shelving attempts.
body: Mitchell Hashimoto says the most common request he got after Vagrant was "Vagrant for remote envs", and he tried and failed to build it many times. About five years ago at HashiCorp he got as far as a website and branding, then pulled it at the last minute because it still was not right.

Rex, he says, is the real thing: a tool for remote development and more than just development, built the way he thinks a proper solution should have been all along. For an IT architect who has lived through every generation of dev environments, this is one to watch closely.

stories.headline: Guillermo Rauch's xeet renders an X post to a pixel-perfect PNG in about a millisecond, in safe Rust and wasm
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: a fun systems hack that shows how agent-built software can tackle work that was impractical for a person.
body: xeet is a hermetic X post renderer: no browser, network, filesystem or system fonts. Rauch says it renders a post to PNG in about 1 ms, and 0.4 ms for Jack's "setting up my twttr", which is 100x to 1000x faster than booting a browser and taking a screenshot while staying just as accurate.

It reproduces Blink and HarfBuzz text shaping, 1/64-pixel line breaking, RTL bidirectional text, 28 Chirp font subsets, CJK, math and emoji fallbacks and the "Show more" rules. Rauch's point is that previewing a post is useful for humans and agents alike, and that this kind of exhaustive fidelity work would be wildly impractical for a human engineer to do alone.

stories.headline: macOS 27.3 lets you grant Full Disk Access to specific folders instead of your whole Mac
stories.why_read: Directly relevant to every agent you run on your Mac: you can finally scope what a tool can touch instead of handing over everything.
body: Apple's new support note says that starting in macOS 27.3, when some apps ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, you can choose only specific protected folders or apps for them. With full access, Apple warns, an app can read, change, delete and export your messages, email, photos and other users' data without asking; with System & App Protection Override it can control your Mac and capture every keystroke. Arin adds that the beta gives clearer warnings, can make apps re-ask for access, and shows a menu bar indicator when one app controls another. Existing approvals keep their access.

Kun Chen, in a post you retweeted, argues for going one step further: a new macOS account type for agents, with no admin, no sudo and no Full Disk Access, that can do everything else without ever raising a permission prompt.

stories.headline: Big money piles into SpaceX: Tepper's Appaloosa raised its stake 17-fold to $557 million, and Saudi Arabia's PIF has 80% of its US stocks in it
stories.why_read: Two bookmarks from you on the same theme: the latest 13F filings show how concentrated big investors have become in SpaceX.
body: Wall St Engine reports that David Tepper's Appaloosa increased its SpaceX stake 17-fold in the third quarter to $557 million, about 7.3% of its $7.6 billion US-listed stock portfolio. Polymarket Money reports that Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund now holds 80% of its US stock portfolio in a single company: SpaceX.

X News coverage of the same filings season reports that Stanley Druckenmiller's Duquesne added about $30 million in SpaceX while selling chip names, and that Citadel cut its SpaceX position sharply. Those last details come from summaries of the filings, not the filings themselves.

stories.headline: Microsoft blames last week's huge Microsoft 365 email outage on a July change that only broke on newer, many-core servers
stories.why_read: A classic cascading-failure postmortem with a lesson every architect knows and still gets bitten by: your load tests ran on the wrong hardware.
body: Microsoft's preliminary post-incident report says a July 2026 fix for its Microsoft 365 network gateway servers passed load testing and deployed cleanly, but caused lock contention inside an internal Windows process that exhausted CPU and memory, and the problem got worse on machines with more cores and newer hardware. Its own admission: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores."

The trigger was two ordinary events at once: Teams failed over to the primary gateway that serves Exchange Online, while almost 14% of gateway capacity was out of service. Traffic rerouted to the next healthy server, which hit the same defect, and within two hours more than 80% of servers were unresponsive. Restored servers were immediately overwhelmed again, so engineers had to patch the patch rather than roll back.

stories.headline: Andrew Gallant ships Jiff 1.0, the Rust datetime library that puts time zones front and center, and promises to keep 1.0 indefinitely
stories.why_read: Already used by uv, Cargo, Jujutsu, Nushell and the Starship prompt, it is a quiet but important building block for the Rust tooling you use every day.
body: BurntSushi, the author of ripgrep, has released Jiff 1.0. Jiff aims to push you into the "pit of success" by making time zone handling central to the API so daylight saving time bugs are hard to write. It is already in production in uv, Cargo, the Starship prompt, fd, Nushell, mise, Jujutsu, uutils/coreutils and as the basis for a Temporal implementation in AWS LLRT.

Gallant plans to commit to 1.0 indefinitely unless a significant API defect turns up, because Jiff is meant to appear in other libraries' public APIs, where breaking releases ripple painfully across the ecosystem. His view is that datetime is hard mostly because libraries model the domain poorly and push complexity onto users.

stories.headline: Carnegie Mellon is putting full computer science courses on YouTube for free, including ML Systems and AI Agents
stories.why_read: The top story on Hacker News this morning, and the lineup reads like your interest list: ML systems, software architecture, AI agents and ML in production.
body: Carnegie Mellon's new CS Learn site offers full classroom lectures from its faculty, free to watch. Machine Learning with Large Datasets and Principles of Computing are live now, and premieres this week include Machine Learning Systems with Tianqi Chen and Zhihao Jia (Tuesday), Software Architectures (Wednesday), and AI Agents with Daniel Fried and Graham Neubig plus Machine Learning in Production (Thursday).

More courses arrive in January 2027, including Probability and Computing and Multimodal Machine Learning. CMU also plans AI tutoring in the courseware, and graded work with an official credential through CMU Online.

stories.headline: Chemistry is actually geometry: how network theory and topology predict what a reaction can do with far fewer parameters
stories.why_read: A physics-and-chemistry essay right on your pinned-post wavelength, explaining why fewer parameters can beat more precise models.
body: Models of real biochemical processes need huge systems of differential equations and hundreds of rate constants that are nearly impossible to measure; the author notes a model of the Krebs cycle might include hundreds of them. The essay argues for better abstractions that depend on fewer parameters, trading precision for robust qualitative predictions about what a system can and cannot do.

Drawing on Martin Feinberg's Foundations of Chemical Reaction Network Theory, it walks through results from network science, geometry and topology that reveal properties of chemical reactions from their structure alone. It drew more than 250 points on Hacker News.

stories.headline: Cornell finds two sheep per hectare under solar panels boosts bees and lady beetles by 38% compared with mowing
stories.why_read: A solar story with numbers, and a kind one: the right number of sheep makes a solar farm better for insects and farmers.
body: Three years of trials at Cornell's Cascadilla Community Solar Farm in Dryden, New York, found that grazing two sheep per hectare around solar arrays raised the abundance of wild bees, honey bees and lady beetles by 38% compared with a mowed control plot, driven mostly by an 83% jump in honey bees. At four sheep per hectare insect numbers matched mowing but vegetation control improved; at eight, vegetation control peaked but honey bee abundance fell 45%.

A second paper describes a decision-support tool to help farmers grow solar grazing herds profitably. The researchers chose stocking rate as the key number because it is something sheep farmers already work with every day.

stories.headline: Energy permitting reform takes "another huge step forward" in the Senate with a bipartisan 70-27 vote
stories.why_read: You retweeted John Arnold on it: permitting is the bottleneck for every grid, solar and transmission project, so a 70-vote margin is a big deal.
body: John Arnold watched from the Senate gallery Monday night as legislation to modernize energy permitting passed another vote, 70-27, with strong bipartisan support. Over the weekend he also noted that the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, Washington Post and Bloomberg all back passage of BAAJA.
For energy tech, faster permitting is what turns announced projects into steel in the ground. The vote is a step in the process, not final passage.

stories.headline: Goldman estimates China's total oil demand already peaked in 2025
stories.why_read: You bookmarked Javier Blas flagging it: if the world's biggest oil importer has peaked, EVs and electrification are bending the global curve.
body: Goldman Sachs published a bearish 2027 oil view on Monday that calls for a surplus, and most of the debate focused on that headline. Bloomberg columnist Javier Blas flagged a line he thinks deserves more attention: "We estimate that China's total oil demand peaked in 2025."

A peak in Chinese oil demand would be one of the biggest shifts in energy markets in decades, and it is consistent with the speed of EV adoption and trucking electrification in China. It is an estimate, not a measured fact yet.

stories.headline: San Antonio has more people than Austin, yet Austin's airport boarded twice as many passengers last year
stories.why_read: A local puzzle for an Austinite, from a post you bookmarked: 10.65 million boardings at AUS versus 5.24 million at SAT, only 80 miles apart.
body: Adam Nathan points out that San Antonio has more residents than Austin and the two cities are only about 80 miles apart, but last year Austin's airport boarded 10.65 million passengers and San Antonio's boarded 5.24 million.

He asks the obvious question: how did the smaller city end up with twice the airport? It pairs nicely with today's robotaxi-versus-short-haul-flights argument: at 80 miles, the competition between those two airports may one day be a ride, not a flight.
